findings.title: The VIX leg compares spot constant-maturity indices (VIX9D/VIX/VIX3M/VIX6M) with the model's forward-starting 30-day VIX, so the published showcase fit is an artifact
findings.description: ^VIX9D, ^VIX, ^VIX3M and ^VIX6M are Cboe SPOT constant-maturity indices. Their squares are (1/tau)·E0[∫_0^tau v_s ds] over the next 9, 30, 93 and 184 calendar days (Cboe 'Selected SPX Target Expected Volatility Term Indices' methodology: 'VIX3M 93 days ... VIX6M 184 days'). Under Heston, index_tau = 100·sqrt(theta + (v0-theta)(1-e^{-kappa·tau})/(kappa·tau)), which is heston_vix_index(T=tau). _vix_futures_leg instead calls heston_vix_futures_curve(kappa,theta,sigma,v0,tenor). That function returns sqrt(E[VIX_T^2]): the 30-day variance over the FORWARD window [T, T+30d]. So ^VIX is compared with model variance over [30d,60d], ^VIX6M with [182d,212d], and so on. This is the wrong instrument at every tenor. The docstring claim at :666 ('these indices closely track the corresponding VIX futures prices') is also false. In contango a 3-month VIX future sits above VIX3M. The windows are also off: 91 and 182 days, against Cboe's 93 and 184 and the project's own DB, which stores tenor_days=93 for ^VIX3M. validate() and the NN VIX training targets reuse the same mapping. The published headline numbers (κ=1.77, θ=0.067, σ=0.46, SPX RMSE 0.52 vp, VIX RMSE 0.53, Feller PASS) are what the optimizer produces against the wrong target. Under the correct specification the same data gives a materially different fit, with Feller BINDING and a much larger SPX error. That makes the project's own thesis (the SPX/VIX joint tension) stronger, not weaker.
findings.evidence: 1) Showcase params from data_store/calibrations/joint_cal_2026-05-31.pkl against the DB market row 2026-05-29 (VIX9D 12.59, VIX 15.32, VIX3M 18.66, VIX6M 21.60): current code gives model [13.61, 15.22, 18.51, 21.40], RMSE 0.528, which is exactly the published 0.53. The correct spot-index formula (windows 9/30/93/184d) gives [11.75, 12.80, 15.22, 17.58], RMSE 2.962. The per-tenor difference is 1.86 / 2.42 / 3.30 / 3.82 VIX pts. 2) Full re-fit in the scratch copy (JointCalibrator('2026-05-31', r=0.045, q=0.013).calibrate()). Current code reproduces the published fit exactly: {kappa 1.7695, theta 0.0665, sigma 0.4603, rho -0.95, v0 0.0127}, SPX RMSE 0.523, VIX RMSE 0.528. Monkeypatching only the VIX-leg formula to the spot-index formula gives {kappa 6.0345, theta 0.0502, sigma 0.7786, rho -0.95, v0 0.0129}, SPX RMSE 1.389 vp, VIX RMSE 1.189, 2κθ ≈ σ² (Feller binding, σ pinned). 3) SQLite vix_term_structure rows: ('^VIX3M', 93), ('^VIX6M', 182). The calibrator uses 91/365 and 182/365.
findings.proposed_fix: In heston.py, add heston_vix_term_index(kappa, theta, v0, window_years) = 100*sqrt(theta + (v0-theta)*(-expm1(-kappa*tau))/(kappa*tau)), with the kappa*tau->0 limit set to v0. In joint_calibrator, replace _VIX_TS_TENORS with Cboe windows {^VIX9D: 9, ^VIX: 30, ^VIX3M: 93, ^VIX6M: 184}/365. Use heston_vix_term_index in _vix_futures_leg and validate(), rename the leg 'VIX term-structure (index) leg', and fix the :666 docstring. If a futures proxy is really wanted, strip forward variances from the indices, σ²_fwd(T1,T2) = (T2·I_T2² − T1·I_T1²)/(T2−T1), and compare them with model forward variance. Never compare an index level with a forward VIX. Then re-run every archived fit (joint_cal_*.pkl), retrain the NN VIX head (nn_pricer.py:412), and republish README:67-75/152, substack:35-36 and the dashboard numbers. Tests: (a) for v0≠theta, the model ^VIX value equals heston_vix_index(kappa,theta,v0,30/365) and differs from heston_vix_futures_curve(...,[30/365]); (b) as kappa→∞ every tenor → 100·sqrt(theta); (c) a regression test pins the 2026-05-31 refit parameters and RMSEs.

findings.title: heston_vix_futures_curve returns sqrt(E[VIX_T^2]) instead of E[VIX_T]; the documented '<0.3 pt' Jensen error is actually 0.2–1.9 VIX pts
findings.description: A VIX future settles on VIX_T = sqrt(VIX_T^2), so F = E[sqrt(a + b·v_T)] with b=(1-e^{-κτ})/(κτ), a=θ(1-b), and v_T following the CIR transition law (scaled non-central chi-square). The code returns sqrt(E[VIX_T^2]), which is a strict upper bound by Jensen's inequality. The docstring and inline comment justify this with 'the Jensen error is typically < 0.3 VIX points' and say the exact value 'requires a nested integration and is numerically unstable'. Both claims are false. Because sigma is not used at all, the curve cannot express the vol-of-vol-driven futures convexity that sits at the heart of the SPX/VIX joint-calibration problem (Gatheral 2008). That is the effect the module docstring says this function quantifies ('THE KEY FUNCTION for quantifying the Heston-VIX gap'). The module docstring also asserts 'Heston-implied VIX futures deviate from market ... by 1.5–3.5 vol points on average'. The project has no VIX futures data (README: CBOE CDN 403), so that figure is unsupported. compute_heston_vix_gap and the NN VIX training targets inherit the bias.
findings.evidence: Exact E[sqrt(a+b v_T)] by quadrature over scipy.stats.ncx2(df=4κθ/σ², nc=v0e^{-κT}/c, scale=c=σ²(1-e^{-κT})/(4κ)), checked against exact-sampling MC (400k draws): showcase T=30d quad 14.5242 vs MC 14.5310±0.0072; T=182d 19.7485 vs 19.7574±0.0130. The code's approximation minus the exact value, in VIX pts, across all 33 archived joint_cal_*.pkl fits at 30/60/91/120/182d: max 1.907 (2026-03-24 at 182d), median 1.097 at 91d, minimum 0.220 (2026-07-03 at 30d). Showcase 2026-05-31: [0.70, 1.03, 1.26, 1.42, 1.65]. A Laplace-transform formula, E[√Y] = (2√π)^{-1}∫_0^∞(1−E[e^{−uY}])u^{−3/2}du with the closed-form CIR transform E[e^{−u b v_T}] = (1+2cub)^{−df/2}·exp(−nc·cub/(1+2cub)), matched the ncx2 quadrature to 6 decimals on 9 cases at 1.3 ms per evaluation (the pdf-based quad took 35 ms). It is fast and stable.
findings.proposed_fix: Add heston_vix_future_exact(kappa, theta, sigma, v0, T, tau=30/365) implementing the Laplace-transform integral above. Split the integral at u=1, use log1p, and guard u→∞ (see the evidence snippet). Make heston_vix_futures_curve call it and keep the sqrt(E) value only as an explicitly named upper bound (heston_vix_futures_upper_bound). Delete the '<0.3 pt' and '1.5–3.5 pt' claims. Use the exact price in compute_heston_vix_gap and in the NN VIX targets, if those are meant to be futures. Tests: (a) exact ≤ sqrt(E) everywhere and equal when sigma→0; (b) agreement with exact CIR sampling (rng.noncentral_chisquare) within 4 SE for three archived parameter sets; (c) T→0 gives heston_vix_index.

findings.title: The Bates VIX leg ignores jump variance, and the bounds exclude the nested Heston model, so the Bates comparison and the dashboard's explanation of it are wrong
findings.description: heston.py has a correct Bates CF and pricer but no Bates VIX formula. _bates_joint_loss therefore scores the VIX leg with the pure-Heston _vix_futures_leg(kappa,theta,sigma,v0). Under Bates the Cboe log-contract definition gives VIX² = (1/τ)E∫v ds + 2λ(k̄ − μ_j), where k̄ = e^{μ_j+σ_j²/2} − 1. The jump term is dropped. On top of that, the hard bounds lam ≥ 0.5, mu_j ≤ −0.005 and sigma_j ≥ 0.02 exclude the nested Heston model (λ=0). The archived Bates fit is therefore WORSE than Heston on the same day (SPX RMSE 5.88 vs 3.83), which is impossible for a converged nested model. It also sits on its bounds (λ=7.99987 at the upper bound, μ_j=−0.005 at the bound) with success=False. The dashboard attributes the degeneracy to 'jump params degenerate on daily data (see Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard 2004)', but this is an option-surface calibration, not a daily-returns one. The causes visible in the code are the missing jump variance, the bounds and non-convergence.
findings.evidence: VIX computed from the Bates CF via the log contract, VIX² = −(2/τ)E[ln(S_τ/F)] with E[X] taken by numerically differentiating bates_characteristic_function at u=0, agrees with the closed form above to 3 decimals. Archived bates_cal_2026-03-24 parameters: code (Heston-only) VIX 23.949, true Bates VIX 24.733 (+0.78 pts). Test parameters (λ=2, μ=−0.05, σ_j=0.07): 20.000 vs 23.292. Bounds corner (λ=8, μ=−0.10, σ_j=0.12): 20.000 vs 47.118. Pickle: {'lam': 7.99987, 'mu_j': -0.005, 'sigma_j': 0.02132, success False, spx_iv_rmse 5.883 vs heston_spx_rmse 3.833}. The Bates CF itself is correct: CF(−i)/F − 1 ≤ 4.4e-16, and bates_call_batch vs an independent Lewis-Bates quad reference has max abs error $0.00087.
findings.proposed_fix: Add bates_vix_term_index(kappa,theta,v0,lam,mu_j,sigma_j,tau) = 100*sqrt(heston_var(tau) + 2*lam*(exp(mu_j+0.5*sigma_j**2) − 1 − mu_j)) to heston.py and use it in a _bates_vix_leg. Allow lam ∈ [0, 8] and mu_j ∈ [−0.2, 0.05] so Heston is nested. Seed DE with the Heston optimum (lam=0) and assert that Bates loss ≤ Heston loss after the fit. Replace the dashboard sentence with the actual reason, or remove the Bates claim until a converged re-fit exists. Test: the Bates VIX with lam=0 equals the Heston VIX, and the log-contract VIX from the CF matches the closed form to 1e-6.

findings.title: heston_call_batch's fixed grid (512 points, v_upper=300) mis-prices short expiries: 3.4 vp error at 1d, 0.8 vp at 7d, 0.18 vp at 14d
findings.description: The Carr-Madan integrand decays roughly like exp(−½u²·w), where w is the expected integrated variance to expiry. For short T, or for small v0 (13 of 33 archived fits have v0 ≤ 0.005, and 6 sit at the 1e-4 floor), the integrand has not decayed by u=300, so the truncated tail and trapezoid error are material. The docstring claims '512 gives < 0.05 vol-point error vs quad' and that the CF 'decays as e^{-sigma^2 v^2/2 T}'. Both are wrong: the decay is governed by the variance level, not sigma. The calibrator keeps expiries ≥ 7d and fits a 14d bucket. The production outage involves SPX daily expiries, and any fix that feeds <14d expiries will be priced with ~1 vp model error. The pricer is accurate for T ≥ 30d.
findings.evidence: Independent reference: Lewis (2001) formula with scipy.quad to ∞ (epsabs 1e-14) using a CF that matches a Riccati-ODE solution to 5e-11. Across all 33 archived fits, S=7600, K/F 0.7–1.3, OTM options with reference price ≥ $0.50, max |IV error| was 1d 3.385 vp, 2d 1.633, 3d 0.879, 5d 0.231, 7d 0.795 (2026-08-24), 10d 0.226, 14d 0.178, 21d 0.091, 30d 0.038, 60d 0.012, 91–365d ≤ 0.0011. Root cause confirmed: for the aug28 parameters at 7d the error drops from 0.538 vp (N=512, v_upper=300) to 0.0042 vp (N=2048, v_upper=1200), and at 1d from 3.385 to 0.180. For the sep11 parameters at 14d the dollar error goes from $5.97e-2 to $2.6e-4.
findings.proposed_fix: Choose the truncation per call. Compute w = theta*T + (v0−theta)*(1−exp(−kappa*T))/kappa, set v_upper = clip(sqrt(2*40/w), 300, 5000) with a fixed step dv ≈ 0.5 (n_points = v_upper/dv), and assert |psi(v_upper)| < 1e-10·S. Alternatively move to the COS method (Fang & Oosterlee 2008) with cumulant-based truncation, or Lewis α=0.5 with Gauss-Laguerre, which is also the fix for the moment-explosion finding. Test: a parametrised test against the Lewis-quad reference for T ∈ {1,3,7,14,30,91,365}d, K/F ∈ [0.7,1.3] and archived params (including v0=1e-4), asserting max IV error < 0.01 vp.

findings.title: The MC is an 'absorption' Euler scheme, not full truncation and not Broadie-Kaya; it is heavily biased in the Feller-binding regime all production fits sit in, and its antithetic stderr is overstated
findings.description: The docstring says 'Broadie-Kaya exact scheme' and also 'Euler-Maruyama with full truncation'. The code floors the stored state (paths_v = max(v_new, 0)), so the drift and diffusion both see v⁺ and the state is floored. In the Lord, Koekkoek & van Dijk (2010) taxonomy that is the 'absorption' scheme (f1=f2=f3=x⁺). Full truncation keeps the unfloored v̄ in the state and uses v̄⁺ only in drift and diffusion. Absorption has a known positive bias that explodes when 2κθ ≈ σ², and that is where most production fits land (feller_state BINDING). mc_option_price computes stderr treating the 2×half antithetic draws as i.i.d. The correct SE uses pair means. For monotone payoffs the naive SE is overstated, so the test's '4 standard errors (~99.99% CI)' is effectively about 6–7 SE. The tests only use Feller-satisfied parameters, where the bias is invisible. The same mislabel ('full-truncation' while flooring the state) appears in risk_monitor.simulate_qv_convexity. Memory also grows as n_paths×n_steps×4×8 bytes: Z plus two path arrays, about 0.7 GB at the defaults for T=3y.
findings.evidence: 200k paths at 252 steps/yr, T=0.25, against the Lewis reference. Params aug19 (κ=12.37, θ=0.0257, σ=0.798, v0=1e-4): ATM ref 110.361, code 111.713 (+7.8 pair-SE), my full truncation 110.175 (−1.1). 10%-OTM call: ref 0.037, code 0.114 (+14.7 SE, 3× the price), full truncation 0.043. Params feller_viol (κ=0.5, θ=0.04, σ=1.0, ρ=−0.9): ATM ref 135.894, code 145.748 (+7.3%, +43.9 SE), full truncation 137.879. Params sep11 (binding): 10%-OTM call ref 0.319, code 0.459 (+11.9 SE). Antithetic SE at ATM: naive 0.534 vs pair 0.366 (base params, 1.46×); naive 0.315 vs pair 0.170 (sep11, 1.85×).
findings.proposed_fix: Implement Andersen (2008) QE with martingale correction, or at least true full truncation: keep a raw v̄ array, use vp = max(v̄,0) in the drift and sqrt, and return max(v̄,0) only for reporting. Fix the docstrings in heston.py and risk_monitor.py. In mc_option_price, accept an antithetic flag (or detect the 2×half layout) and compute SE from pair means. Generate normals per step instead of allocating Z (n_paths, n_steps, 2). Add a test at Feller-binding archived parameters asserting |MC − Lewis| < 4 pair-SE for ATM and 10%-OTM, and a test that the reported SE equals the pair-mean SE.

findings.title: calibrate_to_spx / HestonModel.calibrate index the weights array by DataFrame label, so the loss is 0.33 at the true parameters
findings.description: calibrate_to_spx filters the surface without reset_index. _implied_vol_surface_loss then iterates with iterrows() and uses the row LABEL `_` as a positional index into the numpy weights array (weights[_]). When bid/ask are present and any row was filtered, some rows get another row's weight and the rest raise IndexError. The bare `except Exception: total_loss += 1.0` swallows the error, so each of those rows silently adds 1.0 to the loss regardless of fit quality. The same function uses a hard Feller wall (return 1e10+...), which rules out the σ² > 2κθ region the SPX smile usually wants and makes the DE landscape discontinuous. Runtime is also impractical: each loss evaluation runs quad plus brentq per option (1.8 ms/option) inside DE with maxiter=1000 and popsize=15, which is about 2 h worst case for 54 options. No production path calls it, but HestonModel.calibrate is the documented public workflow (class docstring step 2).
findings.evidence: Mini-repro: a synthetic surface generated from the true params (κ=2, θ=0.04, σ=0.3, ρ=−0.7, v0=0.04), 4 maturities × 5 strikes with bid/ask = price·(1∓1%); the T=0.01 rows are removed by the calibrate_to_spx filter, leaving labels 5..19 and a weights array of length 15. _implied_vol_surface_loss(true_params, filt, S, r, q, w) = 0.3333; with weights=None = 0.0. Loss at a Feller-violating point = 10000000170.0. Timing: heston_call_price 1.79 ms/option.
findings.proposed_fix: Reset the index after filtering (surface = surface.reset_index(drop=True)) and iterate positionally, or better, vectorise per expiry with heston_call_batch as joint_calibrator does. Replace the bare except with explicit NaN handling that counts failures and logs them. Replace the Feller wall with the same soft penalty the joint calibrator uses, or make it optional. Test: loss at the generating parameters is < 1e-8 with and without bid/ask weights on a surface whose index is non-contiguous.

findings.title: The fixed Carr-Madan damping α=1.5 needs E[S_T^2.5] < ∞; inside HESTON_BOUNDS that moment explodes and the pricers silently return wrong prices
findings.description: Carr-Madan with damping α needs the (α+1)-th moment to be finite. For Heston that fails beyond the Andersen-Piterbarg (2007) explosion time T*(p=2.5) when ρσp − κ > 0 or the discriminant is negative, i.e. ρ near 0 with large σ. Beyond T* the closed-form CF evaluated at u − 2.5i returns a finite but meaningless analytic continuation, so there is no NaN and no warning, just wrong prices. The docstring's stated condition, 'alpha*(alpha+1) < v0', is not the correct criterion. Production fits sit at ρ = −0.95, where the moment never explodes, so no published number is affected. The DE still samples this region, and the standalone pricers are wrong there.
findings.evidence: Explosion-time scan of 200k uniform draws from HESTON_BOUNDS: 0.043% explode before 365d and 0% before 180d. Example (κ=0.5, θ=0.04, σ=2, ρ=−0.3): T* = 465d, and already at 365d the batch price is off by up to $1.76 (ATM 278.83 vs Lewis 277.94). Example (κ=0.5, σ=2, ρ=0, T=3y): batch 0.80-strike put = 0.00 vs reference 93.44, and 1y 0.6-strike put IV 0.01% vs 30.13%. No NaN/inf occurred in 30,000 random in-bounds evaluations at T ≤ 365d, which is why this goes unnoticed.
findings.proposed_fix: Price on the Lewis contour Im(u) = −1/2, which is always inside the strip of analyticity for Heston and Bates, instead of α=1.5. Or compute T*(α+1) and reduce α when T ≥ 0.9·T*. Correct the docstring condition. Test: at (κ=0.5, σ=2, ρ=0, T=3y) the batch matches the Lewis reference within $0.01.

findings.title: heston_call_price (quad truncated at 200) is less accurate than the batch pricer and its docstring misstates what it returns
findings.description: The docstring says it returns an 'undiscounted call price (multiply by e^{-rT} for present value)', but the integrand already carries e^{-rT}, so it returns the present value. Following the docstring would double-discount. n_integration_points is accepted and ignored. The upper limit of 200 is tighter than the batch's 300, so this 'accurate single-point' pricer, used by heston_greeks, HestonModel and all MC and parity tests, is the less accurate of the two for short T. bates_call_price has the same hard-coded 200. The docstring also says 'FFT is used in calibration batch mode', but no FFT exists anywhere in the code (see heston-fft-claim).
findings.evidence: Against the Lewis reference on the same grid as the batch check: base params max IV error 0.560 vp (2d, K/F 0.95 put); showcase 1.108 vp (1d ATM); aug19 5.712 vp (1d ATM), versus 3.276 vp for batch. The price matches the DISCOUNTED Lewis price (base 3M ATM within $0.003), which confirms PV output.
findings.proposed_fix: Make heston_call_price a thin wrapper over the (fixed) batch or Lewis pricer, so there is one engine. Remove the unused parameter, or wire it through with a deprecation. Correct the docstring to 'present value'. Test: heston_call_price == heston_call_batch to 1e-8 across the reference grid.

findings.title: heston_greeks: theta is per year though documented per day, vanna and vomma are in variance units unlike vega, and vomma is noise-dominated at low v0
findings.description: theta = (V(T−1d) − V)/dt with dt = 1/365 is an annualised rate, but the docstring says 'per calendar day'. Vega is dV/d√v0 (vol units), while vanna is d²V/(dS dv0) and vomma is d²V/dv0² (variance units). The ATM 'vomma' is therefore negative (−17,176 at base params), which contradicts the docstring's 'convexity to vol'. The vol-unit value is 4v0·V_vv + 2V_v = +739. The relative bump of 1e-4 on v0, combined with quad tolerances (epsabs 1e-8, epsrel 1e-6), makes the second derivatives noisy when v0 is small, and 6 archived fits sit at v0=1e-4.
findings.evidence: Base params (3M ATM): project theta −415.906 vs a one-day $ decay of −1.1395 (= −415.9/365). Delta, gamma, vega and theta match the reference to < 0.01% there. At aug19 params (v0=1e-4), 30d ATM: vomma −72,191 vs −47,824 reference (51% error), gamma 0.0015597 vs 0.0016814 (7.2%). At 91d K=7200: vomma −7,958 vs −4,524 (76%). The reference used a high-precision Lewis pricer and was stable across bumps: −47,818 / −47,820 / −47,824 for 5%/2%/1% bumps.
findings.proposed_fix: Return theta per calendar day (divide by 365) or rename it theta_annual. Report vanna and vomma in vol units via the chain rule (d/dσ = 2σ·d/dv0; d²/dσ² = 4v0·V_vv + 2V_v), or name them vanna_v0 and vomma_v0. Use absolute bumps dv = max(1e-2·v0, 1e-5), and price with the batch or Lewis pricer at tight tolerance. Tests: theta ≈ V(T−1d) − V; vol-unit vomma > 0 for wings; accuracy vs the reference within 1% at v0=1e-4.

findings.title: implied_vol_from_price returns a 0.01% IV for a zero OTM price but None for an ITM price at intrinsic; clipped model prices turn into silent absurd IVs
findings.description: heston_call_batch clips negative quadrature noise to the no-arbitrage bounds. A clipped OTM price of exactly 0 passes the bound check, brentq sees f(1e-4) == 0, and the function returns 1e-4 (0.01% vol). A price exactly at the ITM lower bound fails the sign check and returns None. Downstream, smile_reconstruction_error turns None into NaN (then dropped by nanmean, which flatters the RMSE) but keeps 0.01% IVs as huge residuals. Both behaviours are silent and asymmetric. The Brent bracket also caps IV at 500%, so extreme short-dated quotes return None.
findings.evidence: iv(0.0, S=4500, K=5000, T=0.25, 'C') → 0.0001. iv(price exactly at ITM lower bound, K=4000) → None. iv(lower − 5e-5) → None. NaN or inf price → None (correct). 1d ATM with true IV 600% → None. In the batch grid, the sig2 params at 14d K/F=1.05 gave model IV 0.01% vs reference 8.08% because the price was clipped to 0.
findings.proposed_fix: Return NaN (not 1e-4) when price − intrinsic ≤ max(1e-10·S, tiny). Expand the bracket adaptively up to 20.0 before giving up. Have the batch pricer also return an 'unclipped/at-bound' mask so callers can drop those points explicitly and count them. In validate(), report how many IVs were NaN or at-bound next to the RMSE. Test: a zero OTM price → NaN; an at-intrinsic ITM price → NaN; true IV 600% round-trips.

findings.title: Key tests in test_heston.py cannot fail: parity is true by construction, 'Bates λ=0 ≈ Heston' runs identical code, and no test checks prices or the VIX formulas against an independent reference
findings.description: heston_put_price is DEFINED by parity from heston_call_price, so TestPutCallParity (tolerances 0.10/0.50) checks an identity. bates_call_batch with λ=0 multiplies the same Heston CF by exp(0), so the atol=0.05 comparison is identically zero. The Bates T=0 test uses K=S, so the intrinsic value is 0 and the test is trivial. test_call_decreasing_in_maturity_deep_otm asserts that prices INCREASE with maturity, contradicting its name. The VIX flat-curve test gives spread exactly 0.0 under the sqrt(E) approximation, so it cannot detect the convexity error. The MC cross-check runs only in the Feller-satisfied regime and uses the overstated naive SE. There is no test of any price against an independent pricer, no short-maturity test, no test of the VIX index/tenor mapping and no Jensen test. That is why the critical and high findings above passed 53/53 tests.
findings.evidence: Parity residuals from the code: [−2.3e−13, −1.7e−13, −4.3e−13, 4.5e−13, −2.8e−13]. bates(λ=0) − heston batch = [0,0,0,0,0] exactly. Flat-curve spread = 0.0. pytest joint_vol_calibration/tests/test_heston.py: 53 passed.
findings.proposed_fix: Add tests/reference_heston.py (Lewis quad plus a Riccati-ODE CF) and parametrised tests: batch and single pricer vs reference over T ∈ {1,7,14,30,91,365}d × K/F ∈ [0.7,1.3] × {base, showcase, v0-floor, Feller-violated} params (IV tolerance 0.01 vp); CF vs ODE at extreme params; Bates vs a Lewis-Bates reference and a martingale test; VIX index mapping, exact VIX future vs CIR exact sampling, and Bates VIX jump term; MC at Feller-binding params with pair-SE. Replace the parity tests with parity on independently computed OTM puts (Lewis put formula). Rename or fix the maturity test, and use K < S in the Bates T=0 test.

findings.title: Published docs call the engine a 'Carr-Madan FFT' pricer, but no FFT is used
findings.description: The batch pricer builds an M×N matrix exp(−i v k_j)·ψ(v) and integrates it with the trapezoid rule. heston_call_price uses scipy.quad. Neither is an FFT, yet the heston.py docstring states 'FFT is used in calibration batch mode'. The performance docstrings are also off: '~0.0005s per expiry slice with 50 strikes' and '~160x faster than calling heston_call_price() in a loop'.
findings.evidence: grep -rni fft over .py/.md/.html finds only the README, substack and docstring claims, with no numpy.fft or scipy.fft calls. Timing in the scratch copy: batch 1.207 ms per 50-strike slice; heston_call_price 1.79 ms/option, so the speed-up is 50×1.79/1.207 ≈ 74×, not 160×.
findings.proposed_fix: Describe it as 'Carr-Madan damped-CF quadrature (vectorised trapezoid)' in the README, substack and docstrings. Alternatively implement a real FFT/COS pricer when fixing the short-maturity finding. Update the timing claims from a benchmark rather than hard-coding them.

checked_ok: Heston CF (Albrecher 'little trap' form, heston.py:69-128) matches an independent Riccati-ODE solution (solve_ivp DOP853, rtol 1e-11) to 1.2e-13 relative error. Tested at u with Im = 0, −0.5 and −2.5, T up to 10y, 7 parameter sets (σ up to 2, ρ = −0.95 and 0, Feller violated, v0 = 1e-4). No branch-cut discontinuity: numpy's principal sqrt gives Re(d) ≥ 0.

The Carr-Madan formula is correctly implemented: denominator α²+α−v²+i(2α+1)v, prefactor e^{−αk}/π. Dollar log-spot in the CF is paired consistently with dollar log-strike. The real part is even, so the trapezoid rule is spectrally accurate apart from truncation.

heston_call_batch is accurate for T ≥ 30d. Across all 33 archived fits, K/F 0.7–1.3 and price ≥ $0.50, max IV error was 0.038 vp at 30d, 0.012 at 60d and ≤ 0.0011 vp at 91–365d. OTM puts reconstructed by parity are accurate. 30,000 random in-bounds evaluations at 14–365d produced no NaN/inf.

Bates CF compensator (−iφλT·k̄, k̄ = e^{μ+σ²/2} − 1) is correct. Martingale check CF(−i)/F − 1 ≤ 4.4e-16. bates_call_batch vs an independent Lewis-Bates quad reference: max abs error $0.00087 over 3 parameter sets × 5 maturities × 6 strikes.

Rate/dividend handling in the engine is consistent: CF drift (r−q), discount e^{−rT}, parity S·e^{−qT} − K·e^{−rT}, no-arbitrage clip bounds [max(F−K,0)e^{−rT}, S·e^{−qT}]. Small vol-of-vol (σ = 1e-4) is numerically stable and converges to the deterministic-variance BS limit.

heston_integrated_variance and heston_vix_index implement VIX² = θ + (v0−θ)(1−e^{−κτ})/(κτ) with τ = 30/365, and the κτ→0 limit is v0. The E[VIX_T²] expression inside heston_vix_futures_curve (linear in E[v_T]) is correct; only the sqrt/expectation order is wrong.

BS implied-vol inversion round-trips to ~1e-7 even at T = 2d with prices down to 1.9e-5. NaN/inf prices return None. Lowercase rights are handled. Put→call parity conversion keeps enough precision for prices ≥ $0.50.
heston_greeks is accurate at base params (3M ATM): delta, gamma, vega, theta and vomma within < 0.01% of a high-precision Lewis finite-difference reference, vanna within 0.01%.
MC log-Euler spot step is an exact discrete martingale. Antithetic pairing (Z, −Z) is correct. The earlier odd-n_paths fix is correct. Seeding via np.random.default_rng is reproducible.

Showcase calibration reproduced exactly in the scratch copy (κ 1.7695, θ 0.0665, σ 0.4603, ρ −0.95, v0 0.0127; SPX RMSE 0.523, VIX RMSE 0.528), confirming that the published figures come from the current code.
